prompt: When Go's designers set out in 2007, which speed did they want to fix first?
hint: The 45 minutes in the talk were spent before anything ran.

choices.text: The speed of the build, from source to a runnable program
choices.why: Right. A C++ program took 45 minutes to build; Go programs running fast came along with it, but the build was the complaint.

choices.text: The speed at which a program runs once it has started
choices.why: That is what most people hear in "Go is fast", and the section opens by correcting it: the build came first.

choices.text: The speed of typing, with shorter keywords
choices.why: Nothing in the history is about typing; the keywords are few, not short.

choices.text: The speed of the network between Google's data centres
choices.why: The network was a reason for built-in concurrency, but no language makes a network faster.

prompt: In the 2007 measurement, about 4.2 MB of C++ source reached the compiler as more than 8 GB once every `#include` was expanded. The talk rounds the blow-up to how many bytes of input per byte of source?
hint: Divide 8 GB by 4.2 MB, or remember the bold sentence.

prompt: Building `cmd/go` from an empty cache printed `real 0m21.332s` and `user 0m57.345s`. Why is `user` larger than `real`?

choices.text: `user` also counts the time spent waiting for the module proxy
choices.why: Building `cmd/go` needs nothing from the network; waiting is not processor time anyway.

choices.text: Several packages were compiled at once, one per processor
choices.why: Right. `user` adds up the processor time of all four, so it can exceed the time on the clock.

choices.text: `user` includes the second, cached build as well
choices.why: Each `time` measures one command; the second build printed its own `0.837s`.

choices.text: The virtual machine's clock runs slower than real time
choices.why: `real` is the clock on the wall. The gap comes from work done in parallel, not from a slow clock.

prompt: In Go, an import that the file does not use is a compile ___, not a warning.
Two packages of a Go program both import package `B`. According to the 2012 talk, what does the compiler read when it meets `import "B"`?

choices.text: The source of `B`, pasted into each file that imports it
choices.why: That is `#include`, the C and C++ behaviour that produced the 8 gigabytes.

choices.text: The source of `B` and of everything `B` imports, again
choices.why: Re-reading the whole tree is the cost Go was designed to avoid.

choices.text: One file: the compiled form of `B`, made when `B` was built
choices.why: Right. It already carries what a user of `B` needs to know about `B`'s own dependencies.

choices.text: Nothing until the program runs, when `B` is loaded
choices.why: Go resolves imports when it compiles; section 03's binary had nothing left to load at run time.

prompt: What did `file why` say about how the Go binary is linked?

choices.text: `dynamically linked`, with an interpreter
choices.why: That was `lookup`, the program that used `net` with cgo switched on.

choices.text: `statically linked`
choices.why: Right. And `ldd` agreed: `not a dynamic executable`.

choices.text: Linked against `libc.so.6` and nothing else
choices.why: `readelf -d why` found no dynamic section at all, so it names no library, not even `libc`.

choices.text: Not linked: it is bytecode that the Go runtime interprets
choices.why: Go has no interpreter. `file` called it an ELF executable for x86-64, which is machine code.

prompt: You copy `why` to another Linux machine with an x86-64 processor and no Go installed, and run it. What happens?

choices.text: It stops and asks for the Go runtime to be installed
choices.why: The runtime is inside the file; that is most of its 2,342,001 bytes.

choices.text: It prints the other machine's system, read when it starts
choices.why: `runtime.GOOS` and `runtime.GOARCH` are fixed at compile time; it prints what it was built for.

choices.text: It prints `compiled for linux/amd64 by go1.27.1`, needing nothing else
choices.why: Right. It needs a Linux kernel on that processor and nothing else.

choices.text: It fails if that machine has a different version of `libc.so.6` installed
choices.why: That is the risk for `/bin/ls`, which names `libc.so.6`. `why` names no library.

prompt: Which of these together made `lookup` a dynamically linked binary in the lab? Choose all that apply.
hint: `go env CGO_ENABLED` and `go doc net` each gave half of it.

choices.text: It imports `net`, which can resolve names through C library routines
choices.why: Yes: `go doc net`, under Name Resolution, names `getaddrinfo` as one of them.

choices.text: cgo was on, because a C compiler, `gcc`, is on the lab's `PATH`
choices.why: Yes. `go env CGO_ENABLED` printed 1, and with `CGO_ENABLED=0` the same source built static.

choices.text: It was built for `GOOS=linux`, and Linux builds are dynamic
choices.why: `why` was built for Linux too and came out `statically linked`.

choices.text: Its binary passed 2 MB, and above that the linker shares libraries
choices.why: Size decides nothing: `why` was 2,342,001 bytes and static.

prompt: To build a program for Windows on this Linux machine, you set the environment variable `___` to `windows` for the `go build` command.

A colleague builds a Go tool that uses `net` on a laptop with `gcc` installed, then copies it into a container image that holds that one file and nothing else. It will not start. Going by section 03, what fixes it?
hint: What did `readelf -d lookup` name, and where would that file be?

choices.text: Installing Go in the image next to the tool
choices.why: The missing piece is `libc.so.6`, not Go: a Go binary carries its own runtime.

choices.text: Building it again with `CGO_ENABLED=0` in the environment
choices.why: Right. That gave a `statically linked` `lookup`, which needs no library from the image.

choices.text: Building it again with `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64` set explicitly
choices.why: Those are already the laptop's values here; naming them changes nothing about cgo.

choices.text: Running it with `go run` inside the container instead
choices.why: `go run` needs the go command and the source, and the image holds neither.

prompt: Why did `./why-arm64` fail in the lab with `Exec format error`?

choices.text: The cross build failed halfway and left a damaged file
choices.why: `file` read it as a complete `ELF 64-bit LSB executable, ARM aarch64`; nothing was damaged.

choices.text: ARM binaries need Go installed on the machine that runs them
choices.why: No Go binary needs Go installed; this one also said `statically linked`.

choices.text: The file holds ARM machine code and this processor is x86-64
choices.why: Right. The kernel refused code for a processor it is not running on, which proves the cross build worked.

choices.text: Programs built with `GOOS` set must be signed before they run
choices.why: Nothing in the go command signs anything; the error came from the kernel reading the format.

prompt: How many pairs of operating system and processor did `go tool dist list | wc -l` count?
How many keywords did the program over `go/token` count?
hint: The second line of its output.

choices.why: That is C99's count, from the 2012 talk.
Right: `25 keywords`, from `break` to `var`.
That is C++11's count, from the same talk.
That counts `any`, which is a predeclared name like `int` and not a keyword; it is not in the list.

prompt: Which of these words are NOT keywords in Go, going by the list the program printed? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `class`
choices.why: Right, it is not in the list; you could name a variable `class`.

choices.text: `defer`
choices.why: `defer` is in the list, between `default` and `else`; lesson 36 explains it.

choices.text: `while`
choices.why: Right. Go has one loop, `for`.

choices.text: `chan`
choices.why: `chan` is a keyword: it declares a channel, the concurrency of section 02.

choices.text: `try`
choices.why: Right. With no exceptions there is nothing for `try` to start.

prompt: `items * price`, with `items` an `int` and `price` a `float64`, did not compile. Which line compiles and multiplies them?
hint: Convert before the operator, not after it.

choices.text: `float64(items * price)`, converting the result
choices.why: The multiplication inside the brackets still mixes `int` and `float64`, so it is the same error.

choices.text: `float64(items) * price`, converting `items` first
choices.why: Right. Both sides are `float64` once you have written the conversion yourself.

choices.text: The same `items * price`: the error was only a warning
choices.why: `echo $?` printed 1 and no binary was made. Go has no such warnings.

choices.text: `items * price` after raising the `go` line in `go.mod`
choices.why: No version of Go converts between them for you; the rule is part of the language.

prompt: A Java programmer reads a Go function that can fail and looks for where its failure goes. Going by section 04, where does it go?

choices.text: It is thrown, and the nearest `try` block up the calls catches it
choices.why: That is Java's model. Go has no `try`, so nothing is thrown past the caller.

choices.text: It is logged, and the function quietly returns zero
choices.why: Nothing is logged for you; the value is handed back for the caller to decide.

choices.text: It panics, and `main` catches every panic
choices.why: `panic` is for bugs, lesson 36, and `main` catches nothing by itself.

choices.text: It comes back as a value, and the caller checks it
choices.why: Right. `LookupHost` returned the addresses and an error, which was `<nil>` because nothing failed.

prompt: Match each feature Go leaves out with what you use instead.
hint: Section 04 names a lesson for each.

pairs.right: Types built by putting other types inside them

prompt: Put these moments in Go's history in order, earliest first.
items: Griesemer, Pike and Thompson sketch goals on a whiteboard
The language becomes a full-time project
Go becomes a public, open-source project
Rob Pike gives the SPLASH talk with the build numbers

prompt: A team must ship one command-line tool to Windows laptops, Macs with Apple processors and ARM Linux servers. Its only build machine is Linux on x86-64, and the tool does not use C. What does this lesson suggest?
hint: Section 03 built three binaries without leaving one machine.

choices.text: One build, because a Go binary runs on any system
choices.why: A binary is for one system: `why-arm64` would not run on x86-64.

choices.text: Three `go build` runs on that machine, with `GOOS` and `GOARCH` set for each
choices.why: Right: `windows/amd64`, `darwin/arm64` and `linux/arm64`, the three of section 03.

choices.text: Three build machines, because a binary must be compiled where it runs
choices.why: Section 03 compiled for three systems it did not have; the toolchain carries every target.

choices.text: Ship the source, so each user runs it with `go run`
choices.why: That needs Go on every laptop and server, which is the installation one file avoids.

prompt: Which of these are true of the binary `why`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Combine what `wc -c`, `readelf` and the program's own source showed.

choices.text: Most of its 2,342,001 bytes are the Go runtime, not the program
choices.why: Yes. The source was 201 bytes; the rest is what every Go program carries.

choices.text: It needs `libc.so.6` to start, like `/bin/ls`
choices.why: `readelf -d why` found no dynamic section: it names no library at all.

choices.text: The `linux/amd64` it prints was fixed when it was compiled
choices.why: Yes. `runtime.GOOS` and `runtime.GOARCH` describe the build's target, not the machine it runs on.

choices.text: It runs unchanged on an ARM Linux server
choices.why: It is x86-64 machine code. An ARM server needs the `GOARCH=arm64` build.
